title: الحَرَكَاتُ وَالعَلَامَاتُ الصَّوْتِيَّةُ
blocks: ## Use the chapter at the depth you need
- Build long vowels with ا، و، ي.
- Distinguish short and long vowel length.
- Distinguish hamzat al-qaṭʿ and hamzat al-waṣl.
[callout] Duration rule: a short vowel is brief. Do not lengthen it unless a long-vowel letter follows.
TABLE: Pattern | Example | Sound | Word example // ـَ + ا | بَا | long ā | بَابٌ // ـِ + ي | بِي | long ī | كَبِيرٌ // ـُ + و | بُو | long ū | نُورٌ
[callout] Do not guess from the consonant letter alone: Wāw and Yāʾ can function as consonants or long-vowel letters. Context and surrounding vowels determine their role.
## Double vowel endings on indefinite nouns and adjectives
[callout] Meaning: tanween adds an n sound at the end. In basic reading, it commonly signals indefiniteness, though full case usage is a wider grammar topic.
## Sukun marks a consonant without a following vowel
[example] بْ The consonant closes without a vowel.
The sequence moves directly from كْ to تُ .
[callout] Pronunciation rule: do not insert an extra vowel after a letter carrying sukun.
[callout] Hidden structure: a shadda represents two consonants: the first is vowelless, and the second carries the written vowel.
## آ combines a hamza and a long ā sound
[example] آ A glottal stop followed by long ā.
[callout] Precision note: madda is written only on Alif as آ . It is not a general mark placed over every long vowel.
## The glottal stop and its written forms
Hamza may be written independently or on a carrier, often called a “chair”. This lesson introduces recognition and functional use; detailed medial and final hamza rules can be revisited later.

TABLE: Form | Example | Functional note // أ | أَكَلَ | Initial hamza with fatḥa or ḍamma is commonly above Alif. // إ | إِسْلَامٌ | Initial hamza with kasra is below Alif. // ؤ | سُؤَالٌ | Hamza on Wāw. // ئ | بِئْرٌ | Hamza on Yāʾ chair. // ء | شَيْءٌ | Hamza written on the line.
Always pronounced, whether beginning speech or linking from a previous word.
Pronounced at the beginning of speech, but elided in connected speech.
[callout] Practical reading example: بِسْمِ اللهِ is pronounced without a separate initial hamza sound in اِسْم because it is linked from بِـ .
